Game on the sports feed this cycle: Oaks at San Antonio — One cycle after this page asked whether Wilson Shepard's offense still had another gear, the Oaks found it in Denver. They won their second NBA Cup game 147-114, the most points in franchise history, topping the 135 they put up in Toronto. Oakland led by 5 after one, by 18 at the half and by 23 after three, then scored 42 in the fourth. The shooting numbers barely look real: 63 of 79 from the field, 80 percent, and 19 of 26 from three, 73 percent. The Oaks handed out 40 assists against just 5 turnovers, scored 72 in the paint and 12 on the break, and their bench outscored most starting fives with 56. Five Oaks did not miss a shot. AJ Dybantsa went 8 for 8 for 18, Wendell Carter Jr. went 8 for 8 for 17 with 9 rebounds, Adash Stanley went 6 for 6 for 15 with 3 of 3 from deep, Harry Hayward went 5 for 5 and 4 for 4 from three for 14, and J. Valanciunas went 3 for 3 for 6 with 6 rebounds in 10 minutes. That is 30 for 30 between them. The leading scorer came off the bench. T. Jerome scored 28 on 12 of 16 with 10 assists in 28 minutes, his second big night as the sixth man after his 19, 7 and 7 in Toronto. Austin Reaves bounced back from his 4 of 14 night in Philadelphia with 27 points on 11 of 14, a perfect 5 of 5 from three, 12 assists and 2 steals in a team-high 41 minutes. Dillon Brooks added 14. Hayward keeps forcing the issue. In 19 minutes he added 4 assists to his perfect shooting, and he is now 9 of 10 from three over his last six games. G. Trent Jr. hit 2 threes in 3 minutes and J. Champagnie handed out 4 assists. B. Simmons was a DNP for the fifth straight game, and T. Henderson Jr., B. James Jr., J. Tate and Coen Carr also sat. The Oaks win their fifth straight, move to 9-1 and 2-0 in Cup play, and are now scoring 113.6 a game while allowing 92.0. (the rider lift is real only where a station row says "game day")

Game on the sports feed this cycle: Oaks at KONO — The Spurs handed the Oaks their first ever home loss. San Antonio came into Oakland for a Cup game in front of a 99 percent crowd and left with a 126-117 win, only the Oaks' second loss of the season. It was even for three quarters. The Oaks trailed by 8 after a slow 20-point first, won the second 35-25 to lead 55-53 at the half, and it was tied 90-90 going into the fourth. Then the offense that shot 80 percent in Denver went cold. The Oaks scored 27 in the fourth, lost the quarter by 9, and finished 41 of 95 from the field, 43 percent, and 12 of 36 from three. They also left points at the line, 23 of 32, and turned it over 14 times after just 5 in Denver. T. Jerome was the exception again. Off the bench he scored 23 in 21 minutes, all six of his field goals from three on 6 of 8, plus 5 of 7 at the line and 2 steals. That is 19, 28 and 23 in his last three games, and the case for a bigger role is getting hard to ignore. Outside of Jerome the Oaks were 6 of 28 from three. AJ Dybantsa led the starters with 19 on 6 of 14, 3 of 5 from deep, and 4 of 5 at the line. Wendell Carter Jr. had a 14-point, 12-rebound double-double with 4 offensive boards but went 6 of 11 at the line. Adash Stanley had 14, 5 rebounds and 7 assists, and Austin Reaves had 13, 6 rebounds and 6 assists with 4 turnovers. Dillon Brooks scored 13 but needed 19 shots, 5 of 19 and 0 of 6 from three. Harry Hayward came back to earth after his perfect night in Denver, 2 of 9 and 1 of 6 from three, but grabbed 10 rebounds and added 3 assists in 20 minutes. T. Henderson Jr. got back on the floor and went 2 for 2 in 12 minutes. B. Simmons was a DNP for the sixth straight game, with B. James Jr., J. Tate and Coen Carr also sitting. The five-game win streak is over. The Oaks fall to 9-2 and 2-1 in Cup play, and are now scoring 113.9 a game and allowing 95.1. (the rider lift is real only where a station row says "game day")

sources.name: Eleanor Rivera
sources.quote: Honestly, from the booth, a five-point drop on a crowded day doesn't read as people leaving the station. It reads as people arriving later, all at once. You see the platforms fill up in waves instead of a steady stream, and that's when the dwell time stretches — the trains are there, but everyone's squeezing on at the same time, doors cycle slower, and the whole rhythm backs up. The ledger shows the number that got on. What it doesn't show is the crowd that's still on the platform when the doors close, waiting for the next one. That's not a loss — that's a delay that shows up in the next train's count.

sources.name: Ximena Mehta
sources.quote: Honestly, when I see 12th Street drop like that on a mild week with stuff going on downtown, I don't read it as people not wanting to ride. I read it as people finding another way to get where they're going. That congestion number is low enough that driving doesn't feel like a punishment yet. And the fact that Coliseum and Fruitvale went up? That tells me the riders are still out there, they're just moving to the stations that connect to their actual lives — the East Oakland events, the hub work at Fruitvale. From the platform, what I see is that downtown is a destination, but it's not the only one anymore. People are spreading out, and BART's job is to make sure we're where they're going next, not just where they used to go.

sources.name: Rosario Medina
sources.quote: I can tell you what I see from the platform at Fruitvale, and it's not the same picture downtown is painting. The riders I see every day are the ones who live here — the folks who need this hub to get to work, to get their kids to school, to get to the doctor. The Visioning phase being done doesn't change that; it just means we finally put names to what we already knew. Downtown shedding riders while we gain? That's not a mystery to me. That's a different population with different options. The people on my platform don't have the luxury of working from home or driving in when the weather's mild. They're here because this is the line that gets them where they need to go. The ledger can show numbers going up and down, but it can't show the woman with three bags of groceries who just made the transfer, or the kid with a backpack who's heading to a job training session at St. Esperanza. That's who's using this station. And that's who the city needs to keep in mind when they talk about what's working and what's not.

excludedLeads.text: The downtown ridership loss may be tied to riders shifting to the gained stations rather than leaving transit entirely — the corridor data and the station rows both point that way, but the transfer pattern is not on the record.

The crowded-platforms factor at 0.14 may be a capacity ceiling rather than a demand floor — if the downtown stations are at capacity, the loss is the system pushing riders out, not riders choosing to leave.

unverifiedLeads.text: The downtown ridership loss may be tied to riders shifting to the gained stations rather than leaving transit entirely — the corridor data and the station rows both point that way, but the transfer pattern is not on the record.

The crowded-platforms factor at 0.14 may be a capacity ceiling rather than a demand floor — if the downtown stations are at capacity, the loss is the system pushing riders out, not riders choosing to leave.
